a: Magnification: ratio of an object's image to its real size. Resolving power: measures the clarity of the image/ability of lenses to distinguish two points.

q: How is total magnification calculated on a compound light microscope?
a: Objective lens power multiplied by ocular lens power.

q: What is the purpose of immersion oil?
a: It keeps light from bending (refracting) so it doesn't miss the small high-magnification lens.
Dark objects are visible against a bright background. Used to observe stained specimens and count microbes.
Light objects are visible against a dark background due to an opaque disc. Used to observe living microbes that are invisible in brightfield or don't stain easily.
Direct and refracted light come together to produce an image. Used for detailed examination of internal structures of living specimens; no staining required.
Uses ultraviolet light to cause fluorochrome dyes to emit visible light. Used for rapid diagnosis of specific diseases using immunofluorescence.
Uses fluorochromes and a laser light to illuminate each plane of a specimen, producing a 3-D image.
Electrons pass through ultrathin sections of a specimen. Gives excellent view of internal structures with huge magnification (100,000x+), but specimens must be dead, dehydrated, and sliced thin.
An electron gun scans the surface of a whole specimen, knocking out secondary electrons to produce a 3-D image of the external surface.

q: What are the steps for a heat-fixed smear?
a: Add microbes to a slide with water, emulsify and air dry, heat fix by passing over a flame/incinerator to attach and kill microbes, then stain.

q: Differentiate between basic and acidic dyes.
a: Stains are salts. In a basic dye, the colored chromophore is a positive ion (cation). In an acidic dye, it is a negative ion (anion).

q: Why do basic dyes stain bacteria?
a: Bacteria are slightly negatively charged, so they attract the positively charged chromophore of basic dyes like crystal violet or safranin.
Using an acidic dye, like eosin or nigrosin, which is repelled by the negative cell surface, staining the background instead of the cell. Useful for observing capsules.

q: What is a simple stain and a mordant?
a: Simple stain: use of a single basic dye to view cell shape and structures. Mordant: used to hold or intensify the stain or coat a specimen to thicken it.
A differential stain that classifies bacteria into Gram-positive (purple) and Gram-negative (pink) based on cell wall structure.

q: What are the steps of the Gram Stain?
a: Crystal violet (primary), Gram's Iodine (mordant), Alcohol (decolorizer), Safranin (counterstain).

q: Why do Gram-positive and Gram-negative cells stain differently?
a: Gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains the crystal violet-iodine complex. Gram-negative cells have a thin wall and outer membrane that is dissolved by alcohol, washing out the purple, and take up the pink safranin.
A differential stain used to identify bacteria with waxy/lipid cell walls, like Mycobacterium. Acid-fast cells retain the red carbol fuchsin stain; non-acid-fast cells are counterstained blue.

q: Why is heat required for endospore staining?
a: Endospores are highly resistant to desiccation, heat, and radiation. Heat is needed to drive the stain into the endospore.
